newsitem.title: USA: Tosco to assess restart of Pennsylvania plant - CFO.
newsitem.headline: Tosco to assess restart of Pennsylvania plant - CFO.

text.p: Tosco Corp is assessing progress on work to revamp its Trainer, Pennsylvania refinery and will make a statement on the reopening of the plant soon, according to Tosco chief financial officer Jay Allen.
"We are assessing it now and we'll have a statement maybe next week or the week after," Allen told Reuters Wednesday.
The oil market has been keenly watching progress on the plant as it will be a significant buyer of crude oil and seller of oil products in the U.S. Northeast market.

The plant was bought from BP Oil for $25 million and closed early in 1996 when unionized workers rejected Tosco's plans for making the refinery profitable. The union subsequently accepted a Tosco plan which included cutting union jobs by 100 to 216 (overall workforce to 360) and a $50 million modernization.

"I believe all the union people have been hired, or if they haven't they are about to be," said Allen, though he added that workers will initially be involved in "turnaround" operations to ready the plant for restart.

"We really don't know yet" when the plant will be fully operational, said Allen, dismissing recent suggestions that it would be starting in April or May, ahead of the "early summer" start date Tosco told shareholders and others last year.

The work on the refinery will result in a cut in crude distillation capacity from about 180,000 barrels per day (bpd) to about 150,000 bpd, though it will improve production of gasoline and other higher-value products.

Gasoline production is expected to add about eight or nine percent to the Northeast region's output which, according to the latest Energy Department figures, was nearly 900,000 bpd, or about 30 percent of regional gasoline consumption.
Smith Barney senior analyst Jim Falvey said the return of the refinery is likely to have more of an impact on imports than local markets.

"Sure, the refinery will add supplies (in the U.S. Northeast), but the biggest impact will probably be to reduce the need for some European imports," Falvey said. "As for margins, I see it being neutral or only slightly depressive," he added.
Tosco's chief executive officer, Thomas O'Malley, said last autumn that he expects the plant to contribute net revenue of around $40 million a year.
